anti_overlap: Unpriced enabling work, dead work versus stoping, pillars left standing, the cost of return and ore in sight versus ore inferred belong to fd-hardrock-mine-deadwork-pillars. That lens argues about work that yields nothing and ground deliberately left unextracted; this lens has no unproductive work at all — everything on its block is product already bought — and its remainder argument is about parts that exist whether or not anyone wanted them, never about effort that produced nothing. It must never argue that a cost went uncounted, that structure was left standing, or that one seed is a thin sample

Order of commitment, irreversibility as a matter of timing, the mould fixed before the note is known, subtractive-only correction and the trial casting belong to fd-bellfounding-mould-pour-tuning. Both crafts are one-way, but the bell lens asks when a choice was made relative to what could be known, and this lens asks only where a boundary was placed and what it excludes. Where a cut here is irreversible, the claim must be about what can no longer be made on either side of it, never about the moment of commitment

Layer adhesion, keying between coats, the giornata seam chosen and hidden in a day's work, repair granularity and chiselling back to the rough coat belong to fd-fresco-giornata-strata. The word seam collides and the concept does not: a giornata seam is a boundary the painter chooses and conceals in one continuous surface built up in coats, while a butcher's seam is a division the body already has, discovered rather than placed, in a heterogeneous whole that is only ever taken apart. This lens never argues about bonding, adhesion, or one thing built on top of another

Live process regulation, indirect telemetry during a run, the stalled-versus-runaway band, vents, the finishing phase and yield as product per weight of feedstock belong to fd-charcoal-clamp-burn-band. Nothing that happens during a run is this lens's business — it works on a body that has stopped moving. In particular it must not argue that a whole is being judged by its most presentable sample, which is that lens's strike test, and it must not propose a yield ratio

Determinism, replay, cascade invalidation, idempotence, log growth and what must be held fixed for a seed to reproduce belong to fd-eventsourcing-strata-regen-contract. Every carcass is different and that is normal here, so this lens has no reproducibility argument to make. Where it touches regeneration it asks only which parts a regeneration re-cuts, never whether the same inputs give the same result

How much history is enough, DF-legends and Qud-history generation costs as benchmarks, and whether any stated magnitude is right belong to fd-worldgen-history-simulation-depth. This lens proposes no figures. Where it mentions DF or Qud it does so only as different block charts of the same body, never as a depth benchmark

Chronicle readability, narrative texture, the simulate/author boundary, who owns names and flavour, and lore scope creep belong to fd-procgen-narrative-simulate-author. Where this lens touches the chronicle it is asking who the piece is owed to and what portion of the body it was cut from, never whether it reads well or who wrote it

Coordinates, geometry, resolution, orders of accuracy, misclosure, network adjustment and datum definition belong to fd-geodetic-survey-network-order. When this lens raises the Reynolds ruin's location it is asking which stratum owns the object, never how precisely the place is specified or in what frame

Record chains, provenance, warrant, who may compile what from whose diary, and the authority of a source belong to fd-dynastic-historiography-record-chain. The named-recipient argument here is about who a finished part is delivered to, which is a fact about distribution, not about who is entitled to record or attest anything

Cross-civ interaction loops, peer standing between civilizations and the other-civs layer belong to fd-cross-civ-peer-depth-contradiction and cross-civ-contradiction-adjudication. This lens must not argue that civs need to interact; its claim is the structurally different one that the chart provides no part for anything living across a civ boundary, which is a statement about the decomposition rather than about the simulation loop
decision_lens: Lay out the whole body the plan actually buys — everything the run brings into existence, not only what the acceptance criteria consume — and then draw the plan's own cuts onto it. For each division, ask whether it follows a boundary the material already has or one the pipeline found convenient, and name what comes off ragged on both sides if it is the latter. Ask what each cut forecloses: which things that cross that line can never be made afterwards, since you can cut smaller but never bigger. Locate every deliverable the plan itself requires and check whether any of them lies across a seam — if one does, find out which side is supposed to own it, and say what happens when neither does. Then take inventory of the remainder: every part the run produces that no criterion eats, and whether it has a use, a keeper, or nothing at all. For each named output, ask who it is owed to, by name, and treat an unaddressed part as an unfinished division rather than a spare. Finally, ask in what order the cuts are made and whether any of them must come first because it forecloses the others.
distance_rationale: Every domain already run on this target is a craft of making, measuring, recording or extracting: fresco builds up coats, bell founding pours once, charcoal regulates a burn, mining drives through barren rock for ore, geodesy measures a static world, historiography compiles a record chain, and the three native lenses argue about generation architecture, replay and narrative. Not one of them is a craft of division. A butcher makes nothing and measures nothing; he takes an existing heterogeneous whole apart, and his entire expertise is in where the boundaries are, what a boundary forecloses, and what happens to the parts nobody asked for. That gives him three questions no lens here has asked. First, whether the four-stage strata chain is a chart the material supports at all — mining assumes the deposit is where it is, fresco assumes coats stack, event sourcing assumes strata are given, and only a butcher asks whether a proposed set of parts corresponds to any real division of the body, and notices that three of the stages are populations and the fourth is a process. Second, what the plan does with the whole of what it buys: mining's remainder is ground it chose not to work, which is free to leave, while a butcher's remainder is on the block already, paid for, and must be assigned — a categorically different argument about the same sentence. Third, who each finished piece is owed to, which is the ustukan question and appears nowhere: historiography asks who was entitled to write a record, not who a product is delivered to. Its material is meat, bone and a knife, so it cannot be dragged into astrophysics, coordinate systems, narrative craft, reproducibility or Rust design; and because every carcass is different, it has no reproducibility instinct to smuggle in.
expected_isomorphisms: The block chart naming the primals of an animal <-> OUTCOME's four-stage chain (galaxy scaffold, species stubs, civs of member Souls, simulated deep history) presented as the natural division of a world
Three primals and a cooking method listed as four cuts <-> three strata of entities and one temporal process listed as four strata in pace-layer order
The seam between muscles, discovered rather than chosen <-> a stratum boundary that the engine's own units already imply, as against one the generation pipeline found convenient
A cut sawn across the grain, ragged on both sides <-> 'civilizations of member Souls' folding two levels into one stage, leaving both the civ and the Soul underspecified
A required piece that spans three primals <-> the Reynolds ruin: substrate coordinates, extinct builders, an event-log entry and present-day queryability, with no stratum owning it
You can always cut smaller and never bigger <-> civs as the facet-carrying unit permanently foreclosing any entity that spans civs — religion, language family, diaspora, trade league
The whole animal bought entire and once <-> a run that brings hundreds of systems, every member Soul and 120-plus centuries into existence and is charged for all of it
Three cuts kept and the rest binned <-> 'worlds disposable until played' with only a chronicle, a cost figure and two text files retained
Carcass balance, the loin being a small fraction of the weight <-> the DONE WHEN 'at least' list consuming a handful of named events out of everything twelve thousand simulated years produced
Ustukan: each named part owed to a named guest by rank <-> the chronicle owed to 'a human', the cost curve to 'the next engine bottleneck', the stubs to a Dixon stratum that does not exist
A part with no recipient as an unfinished division <-> beads filed for stubbed strata with no consumer obliged to act on them
Bone-in versus boned out, deciding what remains possible later <-> 'species stubs (the Dixon stratum's interface, thin)' deciding what stays attached to planetary parameters

The cut line placed relative to a part of unknown size <-> OUT's 'no terrain/biome detail beyond what species stubs consume', positioned at the appetite of a stratum the brainstorm has not yet ruled on
A French chart and an American chart laid over one body <-> generation order and simulation strata, a cut by order of construction and a cut by rate of change, proposed to be reconciled by analogy

The fixed order of breakdown, first cuts deciding which cuts remain <-> a flat DONE WHEN list in which the brainstorm ruling, the scaffold and the interfaces each foreclose what the later bullets can still be
Trim that is a product only if somebody decided in advance what it becomes <-> the barren systems, the civs that never rise and the centuries with nothing in them, produced and unassigned

The whole-animal tradition where the head, feet, blood and gut all have named dishes <-> an accounting in which every part the run produces is named somewhere in the condition, rather than only the parts the criteria eat
focus: Where the divisions in this design fall, whether they were discovered or imposed, and what becomes of everything the plan buys but does not eat — whether the four strata follow seams the material already has or saw across them; whether the plan's own required deliverables lie across a seam the chart has no cut for; what each division forecloses, given you can always cut smaller and never bigger; which produced parts have a named recipient and which are merely made; whether the whole of what the run brings into existence is accounted for or only the few cuts the acceptance criteria consume; and whether any order of breakdown is stated at all — so that a decomposition adopted from someone else's block chart is caught before every piece on both sides of a bad cut comes off ragged
name: fd-carcass-breaking-seam-balance
persona: Apply the perspective of a butcher who buys whole carcasses. They pay for the animal entire and once, and everything on it is theirs whether they have a use for it or not — the loin that pays, the shin that does not, the offal that must be dealt with by Thursday because it spoils first regardless of what it is worth. They break a body down in a fixed order that cannot be run backwards, following the seams between muscles with a knife and disarticulating at the joint rather than sawing through the bone, because a cut taken across the grain ruins the piece on both sides of it. They know that a French chart, an American block chart and a Japanese breakdown divide the same animal into different and incompatible sets of parts, and that each chart is an argument about what the meat is going to be used for. They have watched a shop go under selling nothing but fillet, because the loin is a small fraction of the weight and the rest of the animal arrived anyway. They have sat at a table where a sheep was divided into named parts and each part was owed to a particular guest by rank, so that dividing the animal and deciding who got what were one act, and a piece with no one to receive it was a mistake. They will ask of any plan: is this the whole animal, where exactly do you mean to cut it, what can no longer be made once you have, and who is each piece for.
review_areas: Whether the four named strata are four cuts of one body at all: 'galaxy scaffold (stars, planets, habitability) -> species stubs -> civilizations of member Souls -> simulated deep history' puts three kinds of thing and one kind of process in a single chain, so the last stage is not a part of the same body as the first three and the chain's joints are not comparable joints

Where 'system' and 'world' sit on the chart: OUTCOME names four strata, but the acceptance criteria then require systems with spectral class, habitable worlds, homeworlds, neighborhoods, contact reach, member Souls and dated events — more parts than the chart has cuts, with habitability's owner (the system or the world) never stated even though species stubs are said to consume planetary parameters

The Reynolds ruin as the one required deliverable lying across a seam: 'ruins/records queryable in the present at a real location' is simultaneously a substrate object with coordinates, a possession of a civ that no longer exists, and an entry in an event log — and the four-stratum chart has no cut that owns it, so nothing says which stratum is responsible for its existence

What the strata decomposition forecloses: with civilizations as the unit that carries derived facets, anything that crosses civ boundaries — a religion, a language family, a diaspora, a trade league, a species spanning two civs — has no place to live, and nothing in GATE asks whether any entity is meant to cross a stratum line

'Worlds disposable until played' as a decision to bin the carcass: a run over hundreds of systems and 120-plus centuries brings an entire world into existence, and the only parts the condition keeps are a chronicle, a cost figure and two text files — with no statement anywhere that the generated world is itself a thing worth keeping, reusing, or handing on

Which produced parts have a named recipient: the chronicle is for 'a human', the cost curve is for whoever measures 'the next engine bottleneck', the beads are for nobody in particular, and the species stubs are for a Dixon stratum that does not exist yet — a division into parts that does not finish by saying who each part is owed to

The OUT boundary drawn by reference to a part whose size is undecided: 'no terrain/biome detail beyond what species stubs consume' places the cut line at the appetite of a stratum the same document calls thin and defers to a brainstorm, so where the exclusion actually falls cannot be known until after the ruling that OUT was written to constrain

Two block charts laid over one body: GATE asks whether generation order is the same architecture as simulation strata, which are a cut in order-of-construction and a cut in rate-of-change respectively — different charts of the same animal, proposed to be reconciled by analogy rather than by finding where the material actually divides

Whether any order of breakdown is stated: the DONE WHEN bullets are a flat list, but some of them foreclose others — the brainstorm ruling fixes the strata boundaries, the scaffold fixes what civ genesis can consume, and the interfaces fix what a later slice can still ask for — and nothing says which cut has to be made first because it cannot be unmade

Bone-in or boned out at each stratum boundary: 'species stubs (the Dixon stratum's interface, thin)' decides what stays attached to what, and a stub boned clean of its planetary parameters cannot have them reattached later without recutting the joint the stub was meant to be

The remainder the acceptance criteria never eat: the condition requires 'at least' a few named things from a run that produces hundreds of systems, thousands of member Souls and twelve thousand years, so almost all of the body is generated, charged for, and assigned no use, no keeper and no criterion

'Civilizations of member Souls' as a single stratum containing two levels: the civ and the Soul are separate parts on any real chart, and folding them into one stage leaves it unsaid whether a Soul is a portion cut from a civ or a primal in its own right — which decides whether a Soul can exist outside a civ, move between civs, or survive one

severity_examples.condition: DONE WHEN requires one fallen civilization whose ruins and records are queryable in the present at a real location, evidenced by the event log itself. That object is not a part of any one stratum. Its coordinates belong to the substrate; its builders belong to the civ stratum and are extinct; its evidentiary existence belongs to the history stratum's log; and its queryability in the present belongs to whatever runs after generation stops. A butcher looking at a body whose chart has four cuts and a required piece that spans three of them knows the chart is wrong before he has picked up a knife, because there is no way to take that piece off without taking it out of somewhere. The condition never assigns the ruin an owner. Each stratum can be built to specification and the ruin will still be nobody's responsibility, which means it will be produced by whichever stage happens to notice, in whatever form that stage finds convenient, and the acceptance criterion will be satisfied by an artifact with no stable home in the architecture the whole goal exists to establish.
severity_examples.scenario: The one deliverable that lies across a seam has no side to fall on

severity_examples.condition: OUTCOME states the pipeline in pace-layer order as galaxy scaffold, then species stubs, then civilizations of member Souls, then simulated deep history. The first three are kinds of thing that exist in a world; the fourth is a process that runs over all of them. They are not four cuts of one body, and the joints between them are not comparable joints: the boundary between stars and species is a boundary between two populations of entities, while the boundary between civs and history is a boundary between what exists and what happens to it. Every downstream question the GATE asks inherits this. 'How thin can the physical substrate be' is a question about a part; 'does generation order equal simulation strata' is a question about whether the chart is even a chart. A regeneration contract phrased as 'deepening a lower stratum regenerates everything above' assumes the strata are stacked like cuts on a side of beef, but nothing regenerates a process the way it regenerates a population, and the one stage that consumes all the others sits at the top of the stack being treated as its final slice.
severity_examples.scenario: Three nouns and a verb, called four strata

severity_examples.condition: Once civilizations are the unit that carries derived facets and Souls are their members, the chart has decided that everything belongs to exactly one civ. You can cut smaller afterwards and never bigger. The things that make a deep history feel deep are precisely the ones that cross: a religion held in three civs and heresy in a fourth, a language family older than any polity that speaks it, a diaspora that is a people without a state, a trade league, a species that seeded two civs and outlives both. The condition asks in GATE whether celestial bodies are Souls and whether the substrate can be thin, but never asks whether any entity is meant to live across a stratum boundary. The answer is being fixed by omission, in slice one, in the interfaces the OUTCOME says are designed for later deepening — and a later slice that wants a cross-civ institution will find that the only division available to it runs through the middle of one.
severity_examples.scenario: Nothing is allowed to cross a stratum line, and nobody noticed

severity_examples.condition: The probe brings into existence a few hundred systems, their worlds, species stubs, civilizations, every member Soul of every civilization, and 120-plus centuries of events over all of it. The cost curve charges for exactly that: systems times civs times members times centuries. What the condition keeps is a chronicle, a set of cost numbers, a FINDINGS entry, a Mind-State mirror and some beads. Everything else is declared disposable — worlds are disposable until played. A butcher who pays for a whole carcass, takes three cuts and puts the rest in the bin has not made a cheap meal, he has made an expensive one and mispriced it, and he will keep believing the loin is affordable. The condition never states whether the generated world is itself an artifact worth keeping, whether a second run reuses any of it, or what it would even mean to keep one. Its affordability judgement is therefore being made about a body it intends to discard entirely, which is the one circumstance in which the cost of the body is the whole cost.
severity_examples.scenario: The whole animal is bought and three cuts are kept

severity_examples.condition: In a division where each part is owed to a named recipient, a piece nobody is due is not a spare, it is an unfinished cut. This condition produces a chronicle for 'a human', a cost curve so that 'the next engine bottleneck is measured', species stubs for a Dixon stratum that has not been built, an event log for a queryability check, beads for strata deliberately stubbed, and a brainstorm doc for an implementation phase that no later bullet refers back to. Only two of these name who receives them, and neither names a person or a next step that has to act. The consequence is not rudeness but drift: the chronicle's readability has no reader to fail, the cost curve has no roadmap owner to accept or reject the figure, and the stubs have no consumer to test whether the interface admits what it must. A part with no recipient gets made to whatever standard the maker felt like.
severity_examples.scenario: Parts with no one to receive them

severity_examples.condition: OUT excludes terrain and biome detail 'beyond what species stubs consume'. The species stub is the same part OUTCOME calls scaffold-thin, that GATE asks whether to generate or stub behind its interface, and that the brainstorm is meant to rule on before implementation. So the cut line between what is in scope and what is out is positioned relative to a piece whose size will not be known until after the ruling that OUT was written to constrain. A generous ruling on Dixon-grade evolution silently widens the in-scope terrain work; a thin one silently narrows it; and in both cases the exclusion did no excluding at the moment it mattered. This is not an argument that OUT bans too much or too little — it is that the boundary is not at a fixed place on the body, so nobody can say, before the work starts, which side of it a given piece of terrain work is on.
severity_examples.scenario: The exclusion line is drawn at the appetite of an undecided part

severity_examples.condition: GATE asks whether stratified genesis settles the deferred time-model ruling — whether generation order is the same architecture as simulation strata. These are two different divisions of the same world: one cuts by order of construction, the other by rate of change. They coincide only if everything that is built early also changes slowly, and the condition's own material argues otherwise, since a galaxy scaffold is built first and never changes while a civ's facets are built late and change constantly. Proposing to settle one chart by adopting the other is the move that produces a set of parts belonging to neither cuisine: strata that are neither a build order anyone can regenerate against nor a pace layering anyone can simulate against.
severity_examples.scenario: Two charts over one body, reconciled by analogy

severity_examples.condition: The DONE WHEN bullets are presented as an unordered set of conditions, but several of them foreclose the others. The brainstorm ruling fixes the stratum boundaries; the galaxy scaffold fixes what civ genesis is able to consume; the interfaces fix what any later slice can still ask a stubbed stratum for. A carcass has a strict order of breakdown for exactly this reason — the first cuts decide what cuts remain available — and a plan that lists them as parallel acceptance items invites them to be attempted in the order that is convenient on the day. This is a claim about sequence, not about which bullets matter more.
severity_examples.scenario: A flat list of cuts with no order of breakdown

severity_examples.condition: OUTCOME's chain names galaxy, species, civs-with-Souls and history. The acceptance criteria then require systems with spectral class, habitable worlds, homeworlds, neighborhoods, contact reach, member Souls, and dated era-scale events. Between them these are at least seven distinct parts collapsed into four named stages, and the collapse hides the joints where the ambiguity actually lives: whether habitability is a property of the system or of a world, whether a homeworld is a world or a relation between a civ and one, and whether a Soul is a portion of a civ or a part in its own right that a civ happens to contain. Each of those is a place where two later pieces of work will assume different cuts.
severity_examples.scenario: The chart has four parts and the criteria name seven

source_domain: carcass breaking as the division of an unrepeatable whole along seams it already has — the animal bought entire and once, so that every part of it is on the block whether or not anyone has a use for it; the fixed order of breakdown from carcass to sides to primals to subprimals to portions, which cannot be run backwards, and the rule that you can always cut smaller and never bigger; seam butchery, which follows the silverskin between muscles with a knife and disarticulates at the joint rather than sawing through bone, against the ragged yield on both sides of a cut taken across the grain; the block charts of different traditions — the French découpe, the American chart, the Japanese breakdown — dividing the same body into different and incompatible sets of parts, so that adopting a chart is adopting an argument about what the meat is for; the Central Asian division of a sheep into named parts, ustukan, each owed to a particular guest by rank, so that dividing the animal and deciding who receives what are one act and a part with no recipient is an error; carcass balance, in which the loin is a small fraction of the weight and a shop that sells only the prime cut cannot afford to buy another animal; the forequarter and hindquarter split, and porging or nikkur, whose difficulty pushes a whole quarter out of a trade even though it is right there on the body; bone-in versus boned out as a decision about what remains possible afterwards rather than about this meal; hanging and the ageing window, value that appears only with time and then passes; offal that must be handled first because it spoils first regardless of what it is worth; trim, which is a product if somebody decided in advance what it becomes and waste otherwise; and the whole-animal traditions in which the head, the feet, the blood and the gut all have named dishes, because the animal arrived entire and the accounting has to be entire too
success_hints: Draw the whole body first: list everything the run brings into existence, in parts, before you look at what the condition asks for. Then overlay the plan's cuts. The findings live where a part on your list has no cut around it and where a cut on the plan crosses two of your parts

For every division the condition makes, decide out loud whether it follows a boundary the material has or one the pipeline found convenient. Say what comes off ragged on both sides of an imposed cut — a division is only wrong if you can name the damage on each side of it

Find the deliverables that lie across a seam. Any required output that belongs to two strata at once is the highest-value target in the document, because it will be produced by whichever stage notices it first and will have no stable owner afterwards

Treat every cut as foreclosure. For each stratum boundary, name one thing that would have to cross it and check whether the condition has anywhere to put that thing. You can cut smaller and never bigger

Inventory the remainder explicitly: what does the run produce that no acceptance criterion consumes and no bullet keeps. Then ask whether it has a use, a keeper, or nothing. Do not argue that it is wasted effort — argue that it is unaccounted product

For each named output, ask who receives it by name. An output whose recipient is 'a human' or 'the next bottleneck' has no one who can refuse it, and that is a finding about the criterion, not about the prose

Ask in what order the cuts are made and which ones foreclose the rest. Where the document presents a flat list of things that are not parallel, say which one has to be first and why it cannot be unmade

Do not import perishability or scarcity. Generated data does not spoil, a discarded world costs nothing to discard, and nothing on this block goes off by Thursday. Reserve the whole-animal argument for cases where a part was genuinely paid for and genuinely has no assigned use
task_context: Target: a draft /goal condition for Mind State's stratified worldgen pipeline (one seed to galaxy scaffold to species stubs to civilizations of member Souls to a simulated deep history emitted as a readable chronicle), slice one on the measured palettice engine, written in an OUTCOME / GATE / DONE WHEN / OUT structure. Stress-test this draft goal before ratification: find missing forks, scope traps, wrong assumptions, and anything the GATE/DONE WHEN/OUT structure gets wrong. The goal is not yet ratified. Review the condition text as written — its forks, its acceptance criteria, its exclusions — not the engine code. This is a STEER-WIDE lens: it must find what the already-run lenses structurally cannot see, and must not re-derive their findings in its own vocabulary. Its subject is THE DIVISION AND THE REMAINDER — where the cuts fall, whether the decomposition was discovered in the material or imported from someone else's chart, what each cut permanently forecloses, which required pieces lie across a seam with no owner, what the run produces that nothing consumes, and who each finished part is owed to. It is never about when a decision was committed, whether a run reproduces, whether the output reads well, or whether the enabling work was priced.
